narrative:
Your application was carefully reviewed as part of our admissions process, which includes an evaluation of how likely students are to pass the bar exam on their first attempt. Based on the information provided, the model predicted a 51% chance that you would not pass the bar exam, which unfortunately led to the decision to reject your application.

Your academic journey shows both strengths and areas of concern. On the positive side, your undergraduate GPA of 3.7 is actually higher than the average for students who passed the bar exam, which suggests you have a strong foundation in your studies. Your LSAT score of 34 also contributed positively, though it is slightly below the average of those who successfully passed the bar. However, the most significant factors in the model’s decision were your class rankings during law school. Your first-year ranking placed you in the third decile, and by your third year, you were in the bottom decile of your class. These rankings were the strongest indicators that influenced the prediction toward a higher likelihood of not passing the bar exam.

Additionally, the model considered that you plan to attend law school part-time, which is less common among students who pass the bar on their first try—only about 7% of those who passed did so while studying part-time. Your family’s lower-middle income bracket was also noted, as students from higher income backgrounds tend to have slightly higher pass rates, though this was not the primary factor in the decision.

While this outcome is disappointing, it’s important to understand that the model’s prediction is not a definitive judgment of your abilities. Instead, it reflects patterns observed in past students with similar profiles. If you’re still determined to pursue a legal career, you might consider focusing on improving your law school performance, particularly in your upper-year courses, or exploring full-time study if possible. Retaking the LSAT to achieve a higher score could also strengthen a future application. This decision doesn’t close the door—it simply suggests there are areas where you could grow before reapplying.
